Dear Eric,

From my testing, I can see that node.stop() is blocking. But, by reading node.stop()’s code i’m not quite clear what part of it actually blocks.

Just for being really clear, I wish to ask you to confirm: node.stop() is blocking, right?

Over on my side I am in GUI logic code that must not block, so I will then mitigate node.stop()’s blockingness, by spawning a separate OS thread wherein I will do node.stop(), and my GUI logics will nonblockingly wait/poll for that thread’s completion, thereby then knowing that node.stop() and node.close() completed.

In my main thread, I would be fine with a sub-1-millisecond block by node.stop() and node.close(), but not more, in which case I like to spawn the separate OS thread as I suggest here.

Any cue on what’s the appropriate action please let me know.

Hi Eric, thank you very much for your extensive response on this one.

I am running the LB Node in my own OS process, so I am not suffering a risk that the RPC from embedded LB Client to LB RPC Server would be MITMed/hijacked.

In my own OS process/C++ program, I want to query the Bitcoin blockchain according to the convention of a consistent view. Just in case LibBitcoin does *not* implement this, I will smartly emulate it myself.

I want to describe my usecase to you however, to avoid traps and be clear.
so in a given moment, I will make a batch of queries to the blockchain.

Logically, at the **START** of my queries, the Node will be at one given head block that we can call   H or HEAD.

The fact that the Node is at HEAD, means all blocks between and including GENESIS and HEAD are queryable.

I want to do the operation:


var myConsistentView = node.chain();   // or node.chain().giveMeConsistentView()

printf(  “The node is at ”  + myConsistentView.headBlock().blockHash “\n”);


myConsistentView.getBlock(“1928309182309812093182”)         <- this one should succeed if said hash is within GENESIS ... HEAD, and fail otherwise


myConsistentView.getConfirmedTransaction(“18329837498239832094820934823")   <- same here, this one should succeed if said tx hash is within a block GENESIS ... HEAD, and fail otherwise

finally regarding UTXO:s,  so a UTXO  within one chain (GENESIS ... HEAD) is introduced at one block , and then optionally spent at a future/higher block in the chain.

So to get to my higher level question:

Does LibBitcoin implement a consistent view, or do I need to emulate it myself in the way that ANY of the query operations I do, MAY be such that a reorg happened BEFORE it, meaning that the GENESIS .. HEAD chain is **NO LONGER queryable** , and so I need to rinse-repeat by picking up the now-latest HEAD, and then query against that one instead?

(For clarity, I understand that there are transactions that are not in any block, also I understand one transaction can be in more blocks on different forks - i understand all that and that LB does very sophisticated and efficient handling of the same. What I’m doing now is more like a very consistent comprehensive approach to ‘clean’, correct, best-practice blockchain queries so my questions related to that rather than to other LB design aspects /  internals.)
The tx hash and index of an output that is not spent identifies a "utxo".

elements.text: This is boost asio behavior. when join is called no more work is created and once all threads coalesce the join unblocks. For threads under the control of zeromq workers in server, a zmq signal is sent which causes the thread to terminate when not busy.
